document_intelligence.document_summary: Comprehensive overview of core computer network concepts across multiple layers including medium access control (CSMA, FDMA, TDMA, CDMA), routing algorithms (Distance Vector, Link State), transport protocols (TCP vs UDP), communication types (Unicast, Broadcast, Multicast), congestion control (Leaky Bucket vs Token Bucket), Internet Protocol (IPv4 vs IPv6), and network diagnostics (ARP, RARP, ICMP).

concept_relationships: CSMA reduces collisions on shared media via carrier sensing, whereas CDMA/TDMA/FDMA allocate channel access via codes, time slots, or frequencies.
Distance Vector routing relies on neighbor table exchanges and Bellman-Ford, whereas Link State uses link status flooding and Dijkstra for full topology maps.
TCP ensures ordered, reliable delivery over IP, whereas UDP provides low-latency, connectionless delivery over IP.
Leaky Bucket enforces a rigid output rate for traffic shaping, whereas Token Bucket provides flexibility for bursty traffic.
ARP resolves IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses for LAN delivery, whereas RARP reverses this process for diskless hosts.

sections.content: In network communication, managing shared channels involves key trade-offs and functional divisions. When many devices try to access the medium simultaneously, delay increases significantly as waiting times grow during heavy traffic. While system designs aim for efficient spectrum usage, employing continuous power control results in higher battery consumption for devices. Additionally, fundamental protocols operate with distinct boundaries; for instance, the Internet Protocol (IP) features no error control and no flow control. Instead, these essential tasks are left to be handled entirely by upper-layer protocols, such as TCP. Understanding these core characteristics helps clarify how lower-level access mechanisms and network-layer protocols divide operational responsibilities across a network stack.

state of its links with all routers in the network.

2.It measures link cost (bandwidth, delay). 
3.It creates a Link State Packet (LSP) with link info. 
4.LSPs are flooded to all routers in the network. 
5.Each router builds a complete network map. 
6.It calculates the shortest path using Dijkstra’s Algorithm.

  Fast convergence 
(Routers quickly learn changes in network) 
  No count-to-infinity issue 
  Routing information is more accurate 
  Good for large networks

sections.content: Distance Vector Routing is a dynamic protocol where each router keeps a table – the distance vector – listing every destination network, the hop‑count distance, and the next‑hop router. Every 30 seconds (or similar interval) each router sends its entire table to its directly‑connected neighbours. When a router receives a neighbour’s table it applies the Bellman‑Ford algorithm: if a shorter path appears through that neighbour, the router updates its own entry. This simplicity brings slow convergence, higher bandwidth use for periodic updates, and the infamous count‑to‑infinity problem where unreachable networks keep increasing their hop count.\n\nLink State Routing works differently. A router first discovers its neighbours with HELLO messages, measures each link’s cost (bandwidth, delay), and builds a Link State Packet (LSP) describing those costs. The LSP is flooded to every router in the network, so each router ends up with a complete map of the topology. Using Dijkstra’s algorithm each router independently computes the shortest‑path tree. The result is fast convergence, no count‑to‑infinity, and more accurate routes, making link‑state suitable for large networks.

Unicast: 
Unicast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to one specific receiver. 
It is known as one-to-one communication. 
Example: Sending a message to a single person or browsing a website. 
Unicast is reliable and secure for individual communication. 
But if the same data has to be sent to many users, the sender must send multiple copies which 
increases bandwidth usage. 
Broadcast: 
Broadcast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to all devices in the 
network. 
It is known as one-to-all communication. 
Example: ARP request in a LAN reaches all devices. 
Broadcast makes it easy to send information to everyone at once. 
However, it increases network traffic and sends data even to devices that do not need it. 
Multicast: 
Multicast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to a specific group of 
receivers. 
It is known as one-to-many communication (only selected users). 
Example: Online live streaming where only subscribed users receive the content. 
Multicast saves bandwidth because the sender transmits only one copy for the group. 
It is more complex because the network must manage which devices are in the multicast group. 
Conclusion: 
Unicast is one-to-one communication. 
Broadcast is one-to-all communication. 
Multicast is one-to-many selected communication.

diagrams.explanation: This diagram text introduces the three primary data transmission modes in computer networks: Unicast (one-to-one communication between a single sender and a single receiver), Broadcast (one-to-all communication sent to every node on the local network segment), and Multicast (one-to-many communication delivered only to a targeted group of subscribed receivers). Each mode balances efficiency, bandwidth usage, and network processing overhead differently depending on the application context.
diagrams.workflow_description: 1. Unicast Workflow: A sender transmits data directly to a single destination host using a specific IP address (e.g., standard web browsing or file transfers). 2. Broadcast Workflow: A sender emits a single packet targeting all network endpoints (e.g., ARP requests), requiring every interface on the local network to process it. 3. Multicast Workflow: A sender transmits a single stream to a designated multicast group address; intermediate network devices replicate the data packets only along paths leading to actively subscribed group members (e.g., live streaming).

3.LEAKY BUCKET TOKEN BUCKET 
Leaky Bucket Algorithm 
 
It is a traffic shaping technique used to control network congestion. 
 
Works like a bucket with a small hole at the bottom. 
 
Data packets enter the bucket (input) at any rate. 
 
Packets leave (output) at a constant, fixed rate only. 
 
If the bucket becomes full due to high incoming traffic, extra packets are discarded. 
 
Maintains a smooth and uniform data flow in the network. 
 
Prevents congestion by avoiding sudden bursts of traffic.

Limitation: Does not support bursty traffic — output rate always remains fixed.

Unicast: 
Unicast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to one specific receiver. 
It is known as one-to-one communication. 
Example: Sending a message to a single person or browsing a website. 
Unicast is reliable and secure for individual communication. 
But if the same data has to be sent to many users, the sender must send multiple copies which 
increases bandwidth usage. 
Broadcast: 
Broadcast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to all devices in the 
network. 
It is known as one-to-all communication. 
Example: ARP request in a LAN reaches all devices. 
Broadcast makes it easy to send information to everyone at once. 
However, it increases network traffic and sends data even to devices that do not need it.

Multicast is a type of communication where data is sent from one sender to a specific group of 
receivers. 
It is known as one-to-many communication (only selected users). 
Example: Online live streaming where only subscribed users receive the content. 
Multicast saves bandwidth because the sender transmits only one copy for the group. 
It is more complex because the network must manage which devices are in the multicast group.

Unicast is one-to-one communication.

receivers. 
It is known as one-to-many communication (only selected users). 
Example: Online live streaming where only subscribed users receive the content. 
Multicast saves bandwidth because the sender transmits only one copy for the group. 
It is more complex because the network must manage which devices are in the multicast group. 
Conclusion: 
Unicast is one-to-one communication. 
Broadcast is one-to-all communication.
